title: The first mountain, from the top
hookLine: the whole year in one sitting
tomorrow: Year one close: the big lookout

lines: THE TOP OF A LONG HIKE.
cards: At the top of a long hike, people often do something odd. They don't look ahead first. They turn around.
They look down at the trail, the switchbacks, the parking lot like a toy far below, and someone says it: we came from all the way down there?
Their legs remember every step, but only from the top can they see the whole path at once. That's where you are.

teach.b: Here's the whole year in one sitting. It started with twenty-one words, from metta to the Dhammapada: the vocabulary of the path, one a day. Then the stories.
A white elephant in a dream. A birth in a grove. Four sights, a night ride, cut hair.
Six hard years, a bowl of rice, a seat under a tree, and dawn. The Deer Park, the growing community, the hard stories, and the sal trees. The Jataka lives, hares and deer and a generous prince.
Then the practices: metta, the breath, the walking lane, the refuges and precepts, giving, the chant and the shrine, the holy days, the retreat.

teach.h: THE PRACTICES, THEN A WHOLE BOOK.
teach.b: Then a whole book, the Dhammapada, read verse by verse.
Then the depths: the four rooms, the direct path, the Heart Sutra, the koans, the elders, and the diamond vehicle. Three hundred thirty days. Not all of them were good days.
Some you rushed. Some you missed, and came back. The path counted the coming back, not the perfect days.

The Buddha told of a man who reaches a wide river, builds a raft of grass and branches, and paddles across. On the far shore, should he carry the raft on his head for the rest of his journey? No, the Buddha says.
The teaching is for crossing, not for carrying around.
So from the top, look back with gladness, the mudita you learned for others, turned for once toward yourself. Not pride. Not a scoreboard.
Just the plain view of how far you've come. Look how far.

how: Many Buddhists mark the end of a retreat or a year of practice by reflecting on what they have learned, rejoicing in the good done (mudita), and dedicating it to others before beginning again.

o: a pilgrim's long road to a shrine
a mountain, the climb seen whole
a stupa raised on a high hill

games.q: match each camp of the first mountain.

s: the path only counted the perfect days
it counted the coming back, including after the days you missed.
the Buddha said to carry the raft after crossing the river
the teaching is for crossing, not for carrying around.
looking back with gladness is mudita turned toward yourself
not pride, not a scoreboard: just the plain view of how far you've come.

games.q: you've crossed a wide river on a raft you built. you're on the far shore. what does the Buddha say to do with the raft?
o: carry it on your head, out of gratitude.
games.why: in the parable, the teaching is like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to.

practice: If you can, sit longer today, up to twenty minutes, and let the year pass through your mind in no order: a word, a story, a verse, a morning you almost skipped, each one coming and going.
When the sit ends, don't jump up; lean back or lie down for a minute, and rest at the top.

wordCard.voice: Pabbata. Mountain: seen from the top, after three hundred thirty days, the whole climb at once, words, stories, practices, a book and the depths.

carryVoice: Your line: look how far. Every day you came back is part of the view. See you at the lookout.
